quests.sentence: Water boils if you heat it to 100 degrees.
quests.ruleExplanation: If you heat it to 100 degrees uses present tense for a general, always-true condition, and boils (also present) states the automatic result.
quests.nativeTip: An if-clause with present tense states a general condition, paired with a present-tense result — both parts stay in present tense.

quests.sentence: Plants die if they don't get enough sunlight.
quests.ruleExplanation: Die and don't get are both present tense, describing a general biological fact rather than one specific event.
quests.nativeTip: Both clauses stay in present tense, since this describes a fact that's always true.

quests.sentence: Ice melts if the temperature rises.
quests.ruleExplanation: Melts and rises are both present tense, expressing a general truth about temperature and ice.
quests.nativeTip: The same present-present pattern applies to any scientific or general fact.

quests.sentence: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.
quests.ruleExplanation: If you heat water to 100 degrees fronts the condition, followed by a comma and it boils, the general result.
quests.nativeTip: The if-clause can open the sentence instead — if-clause, comma, then the result clause.

quests.sentence: If plants don't get enough sunlight, they die.
quests.ruleExplanation: If plants don't get enough sunlight fronts the condition, followed by a comma and they die, the general result.
quests.nativeTip: The same fronting pattern applies: if-clause first, comma, then the general result.

quests.sentence: If the temperature rises, ice melts.
quests.ruleExplanation: If the temperature rises fronts the condition, followed by a comma and ice melts.
quests.nativeTip: A short if-clause still fronts the sentence the same way, with a comma before the result.

quests.sentence: She will call you if she has time.
quests.ruleExplanation: If she has time uses present tense for a realistic future possibility, and will call (in the main clause) states the likely result.
quests.nativeTip: For a real future possibility, the if-clause uses present tense, and the main clause uses will.

quests.sentence: They will miss the flight if they don't hurry.
quests.ruleExplanation: If they don't hurry uses present tense for the condition, and will miss states the likely future result.
quests.nativeTip: The same present-if / will-result pattern applies to a negative condition.

quests.sentence: We will finish early if everyone helps.
quests.ruleExplanation: If everyone helps uses present tense for the condition, and will finish states the resulting future outcome.
quests.nativeTip: Will still appears in the main clause, with present tense in the if-clause.

quests.sentence: If she has time, she will call you.
quests.ruleExplanation: If she has time fronts the condition, followed by a comma and she will call you, the likely result.
quests.nativeTip: Front the if-clause with a comma, then follow with the will-clause.

quests.sentence: If they don't hurry, they will miss the flight.
quests.ruleExplanation: If they don't hurry fronts the condition, followed by a comma and they will miss the flight.
quests.nativeTip: The same fronted structure applies to a negative condition.

quests.sentence: If everyone helps, we will finish early.
quests.ruleExplanation: If everyone helps fronts the condition, followed by a comma and we will finish early.
quests.nativeTip: A short if-clause fronts the sentence the same way, comma before the will-result.

quests.sentence: Unless you leave now, you will miss the train.
quests.ruleExplanation: Unless you leave now means 'if you don't leave now,' carrying its own built-in negative, followed by a comma and the will-result.
quests.nativeTip: Unless means 'if not' — it already contains a negative, so no separate not is needed in that clause.

quests.sentence: She won't get the job unless she improves her interview skills.
quests.ruleExplanation: Unless she improves her interview skills means 'if she doesn't improve them,' following the main clause won't get the job.
quests.nativeTip: Unless can also come after the main clause, still meaning 'if not.'

quests.sentence: Unless it rains, we will have the picnic outside.
quests.ruleExplanation: Unless it rains means 'if it doesn't rain,' fronting the condition before a comma and the will-result.
quests.nativeTip: The fronted unless-clause still carries its built-in negative meaning, comma before the result.

quests.sentence: You can borrow my car as long as you return it by noon.
quests.ruleExplanation: As long as you return it by noon states the necessary condition for borrowing the car, following the main clause you can borrow my car.
quests.nativeTip: As long as works like if, introducing a necessary condition, and can follow the main clause.

quests.sentence: Provided that you finish the memo, you can leave early.
quests.ruleExplanation: Provided that you finish the report fronts the necessary condition, followed by a comma and you can leave early, the result.
quests.nativeTip: Provided that also means if, and can front the sentence with a comma before the result.

quests.sentence: We will approve the loan as long as your credit score is good.
quests.ruleExplanation: As long as your credit score is good states the necessary condition, following the main clause we will approve the loan.
quests.nativeTip: As long as still introduces a necessary condition, this time following a will-result clause.

quests.sentence: She would travel abroad if she had more money.
quests.ruleExplanation: If she had more money uses past tense had for a hypothetical situation (not a real plan), and would travel states the imagined result.
quests.nativeTip: For a hypothetical or unlikely situation, the if-clause uses past tense, and the main clause uses would.

quests.sentence: I would apologize if I were you.
quests.ruleExplanation: If I were you uses were (not was) for the hypothetical situation, a special second-conditional form, paired with would apologize as the imagined result.
quests.nativeTip: Were is used instead of was with I in this hypothetical pattern, even though it sounds unusual.

quests.sentence: They would buy a house if they saved enough.
quests.ruleExplanation: If they saved enough uses past tense saved for a hypothetical situation, with would buy stating the imagined result.
quests.nativeTip: The same past-if / would-result pattern applies to an imagined future situation.

quests.sentence: If she had more money, she would travel abroad.
quests.ruleExplanation: If she had more money fronts the hypothetical condition, followed by a comma and she would travel more, the imagined result.
quests.nativeTip: Front the hypothetical if-clause with a comma, then follow with the would-result.

quests.sentence: If I were you, I would apologize.
quests.ruleExplanation: If I were you fronts the hypothetical condition using were, followed by a comma and I would apologize.
quests.nativeTip: The same fronted structure applies with the special were form.

quests.sentence: If they saved enough, they would buy a house.
quests.ruleExplanation: If they saved enough fronts the hypothetical condition, followed by a comma and they would buy a house.
quests.nativeTip: A fronted hypothetical if-clause still leads into a comma and the would-result.

quests.sentence: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the trip.
quests.ruleExplanation: If it rains tomorrow is a realistic possibility, paired with will cancel — this is first conditional, expressing something that could genuinely happen.
quests.nativeTip: This is a real, likely possibility about tomorrow's weather, so it uses present tense plus will — first conditional.

quests.sentence: If it rained every day, crops would fail.
quests.ruleExplanation: If it rained every day imagines an unlikely scenario, paired with would fail — this is second conditional, unlike the realistic first-conditional sentence before it.
quests.nativeTip: This describes an unlikely, imagined pattern (it raining every single day), so it uses past tense plus would — second conditional.

quests.sentence: If she won the lottery, she would retire early.
quests.ruleExplanation: If she won the lottery treats winning as an unlikely hypothetical, paired with would retire, following the same second-conditional pattern as the previous sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Winning the lottery is treated as unlikely, so this uses past tense plus would — second conditional again.

quests.sentence: Unless the weather improves, the match will be postponed.
quests.ruleExplanation: Unless the weather improves fronts the negative condition, followed by a comma and the match will be postponed, a passive-voice result.
quests.nativeTip: Combine unless (built-in negative condition) with a passive-voice result clause.

quests.sentence: If the team prepared better, they would win more games.
quests.ruleExplanation: If the team prepared better fronts the hypothetical condition, followed by a comma and they would win more games, the imagined result.
quests.nativeTip: Combine a hypothetical if-clause with a would-result describing a repeated imagined outcome.

quests.sentence: As long as you follow the instructions, this process will be simple.
quests.ruleExplanation: As long as you follow the instructions fronts the necessary condition, followed by a comma and the process will be simple.
quests.nativeTip: Combine as long as (necessary condition) with a passive-voice will-result.
